newsitem.title: SPAIN: SOCCER SHOWCASE-ATLETICO SEEK TO SPOIL REAL'S PARTY.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER SHOWCASE-ATLETICO SEEK TO SPOIL REAL'S PARTY.

text.p: Atletico Madrid aim to spoil the championship celebrations of neighbours Real Madrid on Saturday in one of the most eagerly-awaited derby games in the Spanish capital for years.

Twleve months after romping to an historic league and cup double, Atletico will once again be trying to escape the shadow of their more illustrious neighbours, who need just one point to ensure their 27th league title.
Atletico, by comparison, have only nine championships to their name.
Even if Real lose, second-placed Barcelona will have to beat Betis the following day to start the last weekend of league action with any chance of ending the season on top.
The situation is not unfamiliar to Real fans.
Real have sealed the championship on three occasions with victories over Atletico, and recent history is firmly with the home side.
Atletico have lost their last five games in the Santiago Bernabeu stadium, and are without a league win over Real since the 1991-92 season.
Even last season, when Atletico ended the programme 17 points ahead of their arch-rivals, they lost both derby matches.

In January, the match looked to be going Atletico's way when they took a 1-0 lead and saw Real reduced to 10 men. But the game was turned into a 4-1 defeat by Raul Gonzalez, the young talent whom Atletico had let slip out of their hands.
For many Atletico fans the match was just another chapter in a long-running hard-lucky story.
Often treated as the poor relations of their mighty neighbours, Atletico draw their support from a fairly narrow base in the poorer areas of southern Madrid.
By contrast, Real are backed throughout the city, particularly by the wealthier classes.
The difference is reflected by the contrasting finances of the two sides -- Real budget around 9 billion pesetas ($62 million) a year for the first team, nearly three times more than Atletico.
And the gap is likely to grow as the effects of lucrative television deals and multi-billion peseta sponsorship contracts are felt.

Unlike Atletico, Real have a nationwide following dating from the days when they took five consecutive European Cup titles and became the standard-bearers of a Spain eager for international recognition.
Not surprisingly, the team also became synonymous with the intolerant centralism of the Spanish right, and was the favourite team of dictator General Franco.
From time to time there are renewed outbreaks of the long-standing allegations that Real are favoured by referees and other officials.
But contrast, Atletico fans normally portray themselves as victims of the system.
So after years of playing second fiddle to a team so strongly linked to the establishment, victory over Real on Saturday would be especially sweet for Atletico fans.
